title: Placement V1 — Reading Bank (Core)
instructions: Read each passage and answer the questions. Each item is worth one point. Dictionaries are not allowed.

sections.title: Notice — Library Card (A1)
sections.body:
Welcome to the District Library!

Opening hours: Saturday to Thursday, 8:00 a.m. – 4:00 p.m. The library is closed on Fridays.

To get a library card, bring one photo and your Tazkira. The card is free for students.

You can borrow three books at one time for two weeks. If you need more time, please tell the librarian before the last day.

Please do not eat or drink in the reading room. Thank you!

sections.title: Email — A Weekend in Bamiyan (A2)
sections.body:
Hi Farid,

How are you? Last weekend my cousins and I visited Band-e-Amir lakes near Bamiyan. We left Kabul on Friday night and arrived early on Saturday morning.

The water was very blue and the mountains were amazing. It was cold at night, so take warm clothes if you go! We walked around the second lake and took a lot of photos. A local man sold us fresh bread and tea near the parking area.

The trip takes about seven hours by car from Kabul, but the road is good now. Next time, you must come with us!

Best wishes,
Ahmad

sections.title: Article — Kite Running in Kabul (B1)
sections.body:
Every winter, when the cold winds clear the skies over Kabul, rooftops fill with children and adults flying fighter kites. Kite running, or 'gudiparan bazi', has been a favourite pastime in Afghan cities for generations.

The sport is simple to describe but difficult to master. Two kites are flown close to each other, and the flyers use sharp line to try to cut their opponent's string. When a kite is cut, it drifts away, and 'runners' chase it through the streets, hoping to catch it before it lands.

For many families, however, the pastime has become expensive. A good fighter kite can cost more than a day's wages, and quality line is pricier still. Some older residents worry that the tradition is becoming a competition between shops rather than between neighbours. Even so, on a Friday afternoon, when dozens of kites dance above the city, it is easy to see why the tradition survives.

sections.title: Report — Groundwater Under Pressure (B2)
sections.body:
Groundwater supplies drinking water to the majority of households in Afghan cities, yet the resource is under strain as never before. Studies of the Kabul basin have found that water tables in several districts have fallen by more than a metre per year over the past two decades. The causes are not mysterious: rapid urban growth, the spread of private boreholes, and diminishing recharge as open ground is paved over.

The consequences reach far beyond inconvenience. As aquifers shrink, households that once drew water from shallow wells must drill deeper, and deeper water is more likely to carry salt and other minerals that make it unpleasant or unsafe to drink. Falling water tables also concentrate pollution, because there is simply less water to dilute the wastewater seeping from pit latrines and workshops.

Solutions exist, but none is free. Metering and pricing household water would discourage waste, yet it is politically sensitive where incomes are low. Recharging aquifers with seasonal storm water requires land that city planners have already promised to other uses. What almost every expert agrees on is that doing nothing is the most expensive option of all, because the cost of a collapsed aquifer is paid by everyone, forever.

sections.title: Essay — Whose English Is It, Anyway? (C1)
sections.body:
It has become a cliché to observe that English is no longer the property of its native speakers, yet the implications of that observation remain stubbornly unresolved. Roughly four people now speak English as an additional language for every one who learned it in the cradle, and the language's centre of gravity has shifted accordingly — towards boardrooms in Kuala Lumpur, call centres in Nairobi, and lecture halls in Hamburg.

One school of thought treats this demographic reality as a liberation. If English belongs to everyone, the argument runs, then everyone's norms deserve equal respect; an Indian accountant's perfectly intelligible 'I am having a doubt' is not an error but a feature of a legitimately Indian English. To insist on London or New York conventions, on this view, is not linguistics but class politics dressed as correctness.

The counter-argument is less romantic but not easily dismissed. A lingua franca, its defenders remind us, is valuable precisely because it is shared, and shared standards are what allow a pilot and a control tower — neither of whom may be 'native' — to understand each other on the first pass. Examinations, in particular, cannot grade what they refuse to define. The sensible settlement, unsatisfying to partisans on both sides, is probably a graded one: radical tolerance in conversation, conservatism wherever ambiguity carries a price. Whether institutions are subtle enough to administer such a settlement is, admittedly, another question entirely.

title: Placement V1 — Listening Bank (Core)
instructions: Listen to each track. You will hear each track twice. Answer the questions. Each item is worth one point.

sections.title: Announcement — Bus to Herat (A1)
sections.transcript: Good morning. The bus to Herat leaves at nine o'clock from Gate 3. Please arrive thirty minutes early. You may take one small bag on the bus. Big bags go under the bus. Thank you, and have a good trip.

sections.title: Phone Call — Booking a Placement Test (A2)
sections.transcript:
Receptionist: Good afternoon, TOEFL House, how can I help you?
Caller: Hi, I want to do the English placement test. When is the next one?
Receptionist: The next sitting is on Saturday morning at nine.
Caller: How much is it?
Receptionist: It's three hundred afghanis, and you pay at the desk before the test.
Caller: OK. And what should I bring?
Receptionist: Just your Tazkira or another ID, and a pen. Please come fifteen minutes early.
Caller: Great, see you Saturday.

sections.title: Radio Item — New City Library (B1)
sections.transcript: And finally on the morning bulletin: the new city library in District 10 opens its doors to the public next week. The director, Mariam Osmani, told us the building will house forty thousand books and a computer room with internet access, free for all members. Membership costs nothing for students, though adults will pay a small yearly fee. The library will be open six days a week — closed on Fridays — and, in response to requests from local teachers, it will stay open until eight in the evening on weekdays. Ms Osmani said she hopes the reading club, which meets on Thursday afternoons, will attract young readers from all over the district.

sections.title: Lecture Extract — Taking Better Notes (B2)
sections.transcript: Today I want to challenge a habit most of you arrived with: writing everything down. Students who try to transcribe a lecture, word for word, remember less, not more — because attention spent on copying is attention not spent on understanding. Effective note-taking is selective by design. I'd suggest three habits. First, before class, skim the assigned reading so your ears know what matters. Second, during the lecture, capture structure rather than sentences: headings, arrows, short definitions in your own words. If you can restate an idea in five words, you own it. Third, within twenty-four hours, review the notes and add a summary line at the top of the page — future you will thank present you when examination week arrives.

sections.title: Mini-Lecture — English as a Lingua Franca (C1)
sections.transcript: Let me complicate the picture a little. When we say English serves as a lingua franca, we typically imagine two non-native speakers — say, an Afghan engineer and a Korean supplier — converging on a neutral, simplified medium. Empirically, however, recorded interactions show something subtler: speakers negotiate meaning actively, repair misunderstandings cooperatively, and, crucially, draw on their multiple repertoires when English alone falls short. The interesting theoretical consequence is that intelligibility, not nativeness, becomes the yardstick of success. That reframing has practical teeth: it justifies teaching comprehension strategies over idiom lists, and it predicts — correctly, I think — that the varieties which thrive will be those most receptive to borrowing, not those most vigilant against it.

title: Placement V1 — Writing Task Bank (Opinion Essay)
instructions: Write an essay of 200–250 words. Plan for a few minutes, then write. Your essay is scored by a trained examiner against the analytic writing rubric (task achievement, coherence, lexis, grammar).

sections.title: Task 1 — Opinion Essay (primary)
sections.body: Some people learn English mainly to find a better job, while others learn it to connect with other cultures and people. Which reason is more important to you? Write an essay giving your opinion with clear reasons and examples from your own experience or observation. Write 200–250 words.

questions.prompt: Write your opinion essay (200–250 words): Is English mainly a tool for work, or a bridge to other cultures? Support your view with reasons and examples.
Alternative essay prompt (spare): Describe a decision you made that changed your daily life. What happened, and what did you learn from it? Write 200–250 words.

title: Placement V1 — Speaking Task Bank (Interview)
instructions: This is a structured face-to-face interview. The examiner asks the questions, the candidate answers naturally, and the examiner records the official rubric result. Recording equipment is optional.

sections.title: Part 1 — Interview (3–4 minutes)
sections.body:
1. Introduce yourself: name, where you live, and what you do (study/work).
2. Describe your typical day.
3. Which place in your city would you recommend to a visitor, and why?
4. What are your plans for the next two years?

sections.title: Part 2 — Long Turn (2 minutes)
sections.body: Talk for about two minutes about a skill you would like to learn (for example driving, coding, cooking, or a language). Why do you want to learn it, how would you learn it, and how would it change your life? You have one minute to prepare.

questions.prompt: Structured interview: complete Parts 1 and 2 with the examiner. The official result is recorded against the analytic speaking rubric.
Spare long-turn prompt: Describe a festival or celebration that matters to your family. What happens, and what does it mean to you?
